b: In many ways, Netflix’s “The Hunting Wives” is the Platonic ideal of guilty-pleasure TV. It never takes itself too seriously, revels in excess of both the emotional and financial variety, and celebrates the absolute worst traits of every one of its lead characters without apology. Its deliciously campy stories are relentlessly propulsive, full of utterly bonkers twists that don’t make much sense if you look at them too closely. (But, honestly, that’s part of the fun.)

The show’s first season was a surprise hit for the streamer last summer, mixing steamy sapphic yearning with the kind of stereotypical rich-people-behaving-badly social cattiness that defined the best nighttime soaps back in the day. It had everything: Culture war clashes, brassy Texas stereotypes, frequent infidelity, raunchy, ill-advised hook-ups, petty jealousy, lots of firearms, and even a murder mystery.

The show is utterly shameless, in all the best ways, and its complete lack of pretense frees its audience to indulge in its many pleasures without judgment. And although its second outing is more than a bit uneven and doesn’t quite reach the delirious soapy heights of its first, it’s still an entertaining, turn-your-brain-off ride.

“The Hunting Wives” is based on the popular novel of the same name by domestic thriller queen May Cobb, though so much has changed in the screen adaptation by this point that we’re basically in uncharted narrative territory by the time Season 2 begins.

Picking up where its predecessor left off, liberal transplant Sophie O’Neill (Brittany Snow) has just sussed out that her sometime lover and Maple Brook queen bee Margo Banks (Malin Akerman) was the real murderer of local teen Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe). But rather than confessing, Margo turns to her brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), who confronts and threatens Sophie, causing her to run him over with her car. She hides the body, but her attempt to cover up Kyle’s murder is just one of the (many!) plot threads “The Hunting Wives” must juggle in its second outing.
The Hunting Wives. (L to R) Kim Matula as Nadia, Jaime Ray Newman as Callie in episode 204 of The Hunting Wives. Cr. Dana Hawley/Netflix © 2026

Picking up just a few weeks after the cliffhanger that closed its first season, Sophie struggles with her own mental spiral in the wake of her crime. She signs up for marriage counseling with her sanctimonious, wet blanket husband (Evan Jonigkeit) and goes no contact with Margo, determined to get her life back on track despite the whole murder thing.

As for Mrs. Banks, her role in her husband Jed’s (Dermot Mulroney) gubernatorial campaign becomes more prominent, just as their marriage is at one of its lowest points. To make matters worse, multiple specters from her past (both recent and not so much) resurface, just in time to make trouble for and take advantage of her newly elevated public profile.

Elsewhere, Margo’s right-hand bestie Callie Baskins (Jamie Ray Newman) is set to star in a new reality series called “Married Justice”—it has a very “Real Housewives” but more heavily armed kind of vibe—which introduces her to a workaholic Hollywood producer (Kim Matula) who’s very interested in all of Maple Brook’s dark secrets. And despite their (marginal) best efforts, Sophie and Margo can’t seem to stay away from each other, which leads to plenty of sexual tension, sparks, and ill-advised decisions of every stripe. As the season, both women will have to decide how far they’re willing to go to keep their secrets and where the other fits in their lives.

Unfortunately, Season 2 is packed with so many twists and subplots that the show virtually abandons any attempt at nuance or narrative cohesion. Characters develop in fits and starts, their behavior often driven more by plot requirements than anything approaching emotional depth. A second murder investigation into a(nother) dead local teen, as well as a Dale Dickey-led biker gang with a vendetta against Margo’s family, drag down its early episodes, and a subplot involving Brad’s struggle to adapt to college life in the wake of the deaths of his mother and girlfriend feels out of place for most of the season. (It also features one of the weirdest supporting performances from John Stamos possibly ever committed to film.)

But Margo and Sophie’s toxic bond remains eminently watchable, and the minute the show refocuses on the fallout from their endless string of bad choices—both separately and together—”The Hunting Wives” recaptures some of that Season 1 magic.
The Hunting Wives. (L to R) Brittany Snow as Sophie, Malin Akerman as Margo in episode 205 of The Hunting Wives. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026

Ackerman and Snow are still dynamite together, and their scenes crackle with palpable chemistry. This season sees Sophie and Margo working together in very different circumstances, and the show is at its best when they share the screen, their interactions brimming with unspoken secrets and not-at-all-subtle attraction. It’s satisfying to watch their dynamic deepen in unexpected ways, even as more bodies pile up around them. But while the show’s increased focus on Margo and Sophie’s relationship is welcome, it comes at a cost.

Pretty much every other character is painted with a broader and less interesting brush—the show’s other titular wives are barely present, and the entertainingly catty group dynamics that were such fun in Season 1 are essentially limited to brief scenes involving the filming of the “Married Justice” series.

Tertiary figures like Sophie’s husband Graham, and even Jed to some extent, essentially become caricatures whose behavior suddenly turns dark and difficult in ways the narrative doesn’t always justify. (Plus the sheer number of murders and unexplained deaths happening in and around Maple Brook at this point is… unwieldy, to say the least.)

Still, for all its flaws, “The Hunting Wives”’ second season is a wild, propulsive outing, full of steadily escalating plot twists and bonkers narrative swerves that the binge TV model was made to exploit. While its early episodes drag a bit, the second half of the season finds its footing, delivering an even more outrageous version of what viewers loved about the first installment, with a gut-punch finale that will undoubtedly fuel Internet discourse all winter.

This show isn’t for everyone—and its second season is certainly not the place for newbies to jump in—but Margo and Sophie nation still has plenty to celebrate. And, come on, we all know we’ll be right back here for the drama when the show inevitably returns for Season 3.
All eight episodes screened for review. Now on Netflix.
